questions.learningObjective: Draw a supported conclusion about systematic exclusion in northern housing.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what automatic changes in school organization did to local relief work.

answer.exemplar: The decision turned a legal principle into a program of work that fell on local officials. questions.learningObjective: Draw a supported conclusion about the source of covenant enforcement.

stimulus.body: The plat notes for the tract list a common area of land to be held for the use of the residents only, and record that the streets shown are private and to be maintained by the owners of the lots. questions.stem: The plat and memorandum in your brief files describe a development's rules. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The company could release the covenant it had imposed, which shows such restrictions depended on the original developer's continuing enforcement.
The memorandum shows the streets were later opened to the public, since the release of the covenant included the common areas.
options.misconception: Belief that releasing a covenant opened the land to the public.

options.text: The memorandum proves the covenant was unenforceable from the start, since the company chose to give it up so easily.

options.text: The plat shows the residents had already bought the common area, since the note says the land is to be held for their use.
options.misconception: Belief that the note shows residents owned the common area.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the postwar city needed more housing units than before the war.
questions.stem: A housing office brief asks you to explain why the postwar city needed far more housing units than it had needed before the war. Write a short account.

answer.exemplar: The need came from several pressures arriving together. Wartime marriages and postponed births produced a generation of young households in the late 1940s, and the housing that had existed was both too small and too old for families of that size. A long building shortage meant even a new apartment or cottage was hard to find, and returning veterans, new workers drawn to the cities by war industry, and immigrants all added to the number of households competing for a limited stock of homes. Demand rose while the supply of new construction lagged behind it for years.

questions.explanation: New households, a large birth cohort, and a long building shortage pushed demand well past the existing stock of homes. The account asks why the number of needed units grew so sharply.
questions.hint: Ask how many new households were competing for each home.

questions.learningObjective: Assess how a health report treated the postwar child population.

stimulus.body: The health department reported that infant mortality in the district had fallen for a fifth consecutive year and that visits to the child health clinics had risen by half since 1949, with the greatest increase among families in the new subdivisions. questions.stem: A district health report included in your brief describes a large child population. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The report treats the increase in children as a continuing condition, since it asks the council to build for cohorts not yet in school.
The report treats the boom as ending, since the number of births had begun to ease in the most recent year.
options.misconception: Belief that easing births mean the boom had ended.

options.text: The report treats child health as improving to the point of needing no new capacity, since infant mortality fell for a fifth year.
options.misconception: Belief that falling infant mortality means no capacity was needed.

options.text: The report treats the increase as confined to the new subdivisions, since the rise in clinic visits is given only for those areas.
options.misconception: Belief that the rise applied only to new subdivisions.

questions.explanation: By asking the council to plan for children not yet in school, the report treats the larger cohorts as lasting rather than a passing bulge. Believing easing births end the boom, or that better health means no capacity, misreads it.
questions.hint: Ask what the council is asked to plan for.
